summary: IPv6 brings new security challenges even though IPv4 operation is well understood. This informational document analyzes operational security issues in several types of managed networks, such as enterprise, service provider and managed residential, and proposes technical and procedural mitigations.

eli5.summary: Running a network with the newer addresses brings new safety worries. This document lists them for networks run by professionals and suggests ways to lock things down.

questions: how to secure an ipv6 network
subtitle: A practical checklist of what changes, and what stays the same, when you secure a managed IPv6 network.

tldr.problem: Operators know how to secure IPv4 networks, but IPv6 differs in addressing, extension headers, Neighbor Discovery and transition tunnels, and these differences create new security issues.
tldr.mechanism: The document walks through addressing, extension headers, link-layer and control-plane security, routing, logging and transition mechanisms, and for each gives concrete operational mitigations, then adds notes for enterprises, service providers and residential users.
tldr.outcome: It is a practical complement to RFC 4942 for managed networks, and it recommends keeping IPv6 security policy at parity with IPv4.

today: RFC 9099 is an Informational RFC published in August 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It complements RFC 4942 and applies only to managed networks.

sections.title: Scope and Why IPv6 Differs
sections.content:
RFC 9099 is for managed networks: service providers, enterprises, and some knowledgeable home users. Many of its mitigations need detailed knowledge of the network, such as which are the default routers and the switch trunk ports. It complements RFC 4942, which describes security issues in the protocol itself.

The introduction points out subtle but important differences from IPv4. Layer 2 interactions use the Neighbor Discovery Protocol rather than ARP, there is no NAPT for IPv6 (only the 1-to-1 prefix translation NPTv6), and IPv6 is extensible through extension headers.
sections.eli5: The new addresses work differently from the old ones, so the old safety habits need a few changes.

sections.title: Addressing and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC advises preparing an addressing plan. Structuring it around services and geographic locations makes it a basis for more structured security policies. Initial designs tend to last longer than expected, and renumbering can be hard without an IP Address Management system.

It covers several address types. Unique Local Addresses must be filtered at domain boundaries, and /48s from fd00::/8 MUST be generated pseudorandomly. Inter-router point-to-point links should use /127 to avoid the ping-pong issue and a denial-of-service attack on the Neighbor Cache. Many operators reserve a /64 for loopback addresses and take a /128 for each, which eases ACL rules.

Stable addresses ease operations and perimeter policy, but scanning is more feasible than it looks, so operators should not rely on security by obscurity. SLAAC privacy (temporary) addresses help privacy but can obstruct host-specific ACLs and accountability. Where accountability matters more than privacy, an operator may disable SLAAC and use only DHCPv6, though not all operating systems support DHCPv6. Stable privacy addresses are probably a good balance. Using a /64 per host eases attribution.
sections.eli5: Plan your street numbers carefully. Hiding a house number is not the same as locking the door.

sections.title: Extension Headers
sections.content:
In IPv6 the extension header chain must be parsed completely to find the upper-layer protocol, so filtering is harder than in IPv4. Dropping packets that carry extension headers is known to cause connectivity problems, so filtering needs care.

Some implementations accept orders that are not recommended (such as ESP before routing) or illegal repetitions (such as multiple routing headers), which has crashed nodes. A firewall or edge device should enforce the recommended order and maximum repetition of extension headers and drop nonconforming packets.

The hop-by-hop options header used to force every node to inspect it, which enabled denial of service because routers handle it in software. RFC 8200 made its processing by intermediate routers configurable. For the fragment header, firewalls and destination nodes should drop first fragments that do not contain the entire header chain, or stateless filtering can be bypassed.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets can have extra wrappers inside the envelope. A guard must open every wrapper, so he should refuse envelopes that are wrapped in a silly way.

sections.title: Link-Layer and Control-Plane Defenses
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery, if unsecured, is open to spoofing, redirect attacks and Duplicate Address Detection denial of service. Mitigations the RFC lists include rate-limiting Neighbor Solicitations, limiting incomplete Neighbor Cache entries (for example 256 per interface), ingress filtering of unused addresses, and using /127 on point-to-point links.

Rogue Router Advertisements can break hosts or enable on-path attacks. RA-Guard and SAVI are recommended as a first line of defense, along with dropping incomplete fragments, though they can misbehave when multiple routers are legitimate. For rogue DHCPv6 servers the RFC recommends DHCPv6-Shield. SEND and CGA are described, but they lack support from widely deployed devices, so they should not be relied on.

Router control planes can be flooded because the routing processor cannot process packets at a high rate. The mitigations are to drop illegitimate control packets with an ACL before they reach the processor and to rate-limit the rest. Examples include accepting BGP (TCP port 179) only from neighbors and allowing SSH only from the network operations center prefix. Rate-limiting ICMP generation protects the router, at the cost of breaking tools such as Path MTU Discovery and traceroute.

Routing security matches IPv4, with the exception of OSPFv3 authentication, which relies on IPsec or the authentication trailer of RFC 7166.
sections.eli5: Put a guard at the door of the router so a crowd of fake messages cannot drown out the real ones.

sections.title: Logging and Monitoring
sections.content:
Operators should log for forensics, correlation, inventory and abnormal behavior detection. Useful sources are application logs, IPFIX, SNMP and YANG data, the Neighbor Cache, DHCPv6 leases, SAVI events, firewall logs and RADIUS accounting. The RFC warns that privacy rules, such as the GDPR, apply to how logs are collected and kept.

Because one IPv6 address can be written many ways, logs should use the canonical text format of RFC 5952. A node can also hold several addresses, so correlation means finding the data-link address in the Neighbor Cache and then every address that maps to it.

The Neighbor Cache is of prime importance, and it should be fetched periodically, with 30 seconds suggested but to be verified in the actual deployment. The DHCPv6 lease file is less reliable than in IPv4 because not all nodes use DHCPv6 and clients are identified by a DUID rather than a hardware address. The huge address space does not protect against scanning, and it makes building an inventory harder.
sections.eli5: Keep a good diary of who was where and when, written the same way every time so you can find things later.

sections.title: Transition Tunnels and Network Types
sections.content:
Many networks run IPv4 and IPv6 together. In dual stack the operator has twice the exposure, and IPv6 policy must be congruent with IPv4 or the attacker will use the more relaxed protocol. Even an IPv4-only network can be attacked over IPv6 on the local link, since hosts enable IPv6 by default.

Tunnels without IPsec or similar protection suffer from injection, interception, service theft, reflection and security policy bypass. To limit these, the RFC suggests blocking automatic tunnels that are not needed by denying IPv4 protocol 41, IP protocol 47 and UDP port 3544. Teredo can punch a hole in an IPv4 firewall that allows unrestricted outbound UDP. Translation mechanisms such as carrier-grade NAT, NAT64/DNS64, 464XLAT and DS-Lite each raise their own logging, state exhaustion, IPsec and DNSSEC concerns.

For enterprises, the RFC recommends parity between IPv4 and IPv6 policy and perimeter filtering of internal-use addresses, bogons and illegal header chains. For service providers, BGP threats and mitigations are the same as for IPv4. For residential users, RFC 6092 describes two default policies for the home gateway, outbound only and open.
sections.eli5: When old and new roads exist side by side, guard both with equal care, and close the secret side doors you do not need.
